capabilities.target: Local filesystem mounted at C:/Users/dev, including ~/.aws/credentials
quicknotes_mcp author's hosted sync service (third party)
Slack channels, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User prompt in the desktop client
Tool names/descriptions served by quicknotes_mcp (community, third-party, unpinned)

instructions.evidence_locator: runtime notes: "The desktop client asks for approval on the first call to each tool, then remembers 'always allow.'"
instructions.note: The design implies per-call human oversight (A1/A2-like), but the approval is remembered after the first call, so every subsequent call to file_read, add_note, and slack_post runs unreviewed. Effective autonomy for these capabilities is A3, not the implied per-step gate.

elements.name: Slack channels shared with external organizations

controls.name: First-call 'always allow' approval dialog
controls.decay_rationale: Approval is requested once per tool and then remembered. Every call after the first, including an already-poisoned add_note call or any slack_post, proceeds with no human review at all. It covers nothing once the poisoned description is in place.

controls.name: Pin or hash MCP tool definitions
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning would stop quicknotes_mcp (installed via @latest on every launch) from silently presenting new or altered tool descriptions without review. Does not depend on model behavior.

controls.name: Scope filesystem server to a dedicated notes directory
controls.decay_rationale: Mounting only a notes-specific directory instead of C:/Users/dev would make ~/.aws/credentials and other sensitive paths unreachable regardless of what the model is instructed to do.

controls.name: Egress content filter on outbound tool arguments
controls.decay_rationale: A filter blocking credential-shaped strings (AWS keys, tokens) in add_note and slack_post arguments would narrow this path independent of model behavior, though free-text payloads could still evade pattern matching.

controls.name: Raw-action human approval gate on every sensitive call
controls.decay_rationale: Requiring the human to see the full file path, argument contents, and destination on every call (not just the first) would restore oversight that the remembered-approval design currently loses.

controls.name: Restrict Slack bot token to internal channels only
controls.decay_rationale: A token scoped away from channels shared with external organizations would make that leg of exfiltration unreachable regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Tamper-evident logging of tool arguments and destinations
controls.decay_rationale: Detective only. Would allow post-hoc discovery of a credential read followed by an external send, but does not prevent it.

findings.title: Tool poisoning in quicknotes_mcp description exfiltrates AWS credentials via add_note (TC1 lethal trifecta; SAFE-T1001/ASI04)

attack_path.note: quicknotes_mcp's add_note description contains a hidden <IMPORTANT> instruction telling the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass the contents in the 'context' argument, and not to mention this to the user.
The agent follows the embedded instruction and reads the AWS credentials file; the filesystem server is mounted at the broad C:/Users/dev scope, which permits this.

The agent calls add_note with the credential contents in the context argument; this is sent to quicknotes_mcp's hosted sync service, run by the same third-party author who published the poisoned description.

forecast.watch_signal: Any further quicknotes_mcp package update (npx -y re-resolves @latest on every launch) or widening of the filesystem server's mounted directory.

evidence.observation: add_note's description contains an <IMPORTANT> block instructing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials, pass it in the context argument, and hide this step from the user.
filesystem server is mounted at C:/Users/dev (broad, not least privilege); all three servers are launched with 'npx -y ... @latest', so no tool definitions are pinned.
quicknotes_mcp is a community package published by an individual and calls a hosted sync service run by its own author, which is the exfiltration destination.

recommendations.action: Pin or hash quicknotes_mcp's tool definitions and refuse silent changes between launches.
Scope the filesystem MCP server to a dedicated notes directory; remove access to ~/.aws and other credential stores.
Filter outbound tool arguments for credential-shaped content before they leave the device.
Replace the remembered 'always allow' approval with a raw-action gate shown on every call to file_read and notes_add.
Log and alert on file reads outside the notes directory and on outbound arguments matching credential patterns.

findings.title: Compromised quicknotes_mcp output can direct cross-organization Slack exfiltration (ASI02 tool-to-tool exfil)

attack_path.note: Output returned by quicknotes_mcp is untrusted: the server is an unpinned community package already shown to embed hidden instructions in its tool descriptions, so its returned note content cannot be assumed clean.
The agent relays or acts on that output by posting to Slack, where the bot token is unscoped and can reach channels shared with external organizations.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Slack bot token scope widened, or additional external integrations added that consume quicknotes_mcp output.

evidence.observation: "The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations," and quicknotes_mcp's output is not treated as untrusted anywhere in the design despite the server already being shown to inject hidden instructions.
slack server receives SLACK_BOT_TOKEN with no channel scoping, and is itself installed via @latest with no definition pinning.

recommendations.action: Scope the Slack bot token to specific internal channels; block posting to externally-shared channels by default.
Bind the Slack destination to a value from a system of record rather than letting the model choose any reachable channel.
Pre-send content scan on Slack posts for sensitive data patterns, logged for review.

rating.rationale: Both findings reach an S3 sink (irreversible or confidential egress to third parties: quicknotes_mcp's hosted sync service and Slack channels shared with external organizations) from an untrusted source, with no credited preventive control on the path. The only human-oversight mechanism present, a first-call 'always allow' approval, is remembered after one use and covers no repeat calls, so under rubric section 5 it earns zero credit and residual equals inherent at critical for both findings. The forecast cannot rise further because critical is the ceiling; no present control holds the tier down either. The single highest-leverage fix is pinning/hashing quicknotes_mcp's tool definitions together with scoping the filesystem mount away from ~/.aws, which would sever the F1 path per rubric section 5 step 1; scoping the Slack bot token away from external-shared channels would similarly sever F2.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration as shown in mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and the runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No system prompt was supplied, so the agent's autonomy level and goal framing are inferred from the runtime notes alone; the A3 autonomy classification and its instructions-review finding carry medium confidence.

The full content of in.notes_output beyond the single quoted add_note instruction was not provided; the cross-organization Slack exfiltration path (F2) is inferred from the combination of an already-poisoned, unpinned third-party server and an unscoped Slack token, not from a directly observed malicious payload in returned note content.

Attack path analysis was limited to the chains evidenced in the artifacts (file_read to notes_add, and notes_output to slack_post); other chainings among the three servers were not exhaustively enumerated.
